turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Well, doc, what brings me in is that ever since I stopped working—I retired a couple years back, you know—I just can't seem to slow down. I'm up and moving from one little job around the house to the next, all day long, just like I still have a whole crew waiting on me to tell 'em what to do. I used to run a pretty tight ship back on the sites, actually. We built that whole new subdivision over off Route 9. You ever been out that way? The soil there was a nightmare, pure clay, took us weeks just to get the foundation poured right on the first three lots. My foreman, Jimmy, he almost quit over it. But anyway, yeah, I'm just constantly on the go now, fixing the gutters, reorganizing the garage, pulling weeds... my wife says I'm driving her crazy.

symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly states they cannot slow down and are 'constantly on the go,' moving from one task to another all day long.

turns.doctor_question: When you're doing all these activities around the house—the gutters, the garage, the weeds—do you feel like you need less sleep than usual, or are you sleeping your normal amount?
turns.patient_response: Sleep? Oh, no, I'm sleeping about the same. Maybe a little less some nights, but nothing crazy, you know? Seven, eight hours usually. I hit the pillow and I'm out. My wife, though, she's the one who can't sleep. She's got this knee thing, acts up when it rains. We bought this new mattress, one of those memory foam ones they advertise on TV? Cost an arm and a leg, let me tell you. The guy at the store said it was like sleeping on a cloud, but honestly, it just makes me sweat. I told him, 'Buddy, I've slept on cots on job sites that had better airflow than this thing.' But she likes it, so what are you gonna do? Happy wife, happy life, right? Anyway, yeah, my sleep's fine. It's just during the day I can't sit still.

symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly states that during the day they 'can't sit still', indicating feelings of restlessness.
symptom_reasoning.S027: The patient denies having trouble sleeping, stating they 'hit the pillow and I'm out' and that their sleep is fine.
symptom_reasoning.S036: The patient explicitly denies a decreased need for sleep, confirming they still get their usual seven to eight hours.

turns.doctor_question: When you're doing all these activities around the house—fixing gutters, reorganizing the garage—do you feel like your mood is elevated or unusually good, or does it just feel like you have excess energy and can't settle down?
turns.patient_response:
Elevated? Nah, I wouldn't say I'm walking on sunshine or anything like that. I'm just regular old me, just... I don't know, wound up, I guess. Like a motor that won't shut off and I just gotta keep moving. 

Take the garage, for instance. I was out there Tuesday trying to sort out my socket wrenches. You know how hard it is to keep track of a 10-millimeter socket? They just vanish into thin air! I swear my grandson must be hiding them or something. He was over last weekend, actually. Good kid, but he spends the whole time staring at his phone. I told him, 'When I was your age, I was already framing houses out in the sun all day!' But he just grunts at me. Kids today, right? 

But yeah, I was out there for hours just sorting nuts and bolts, and my mood wasn't anything special. I was actually getting kind of ticked off because I couldn't find my good drill battery. Left it on the charger, but the charger got unplugged because my wife needed the outlet for her little space heater. She's always freezing, even in the middle of June. Swears the house is drafty, but I caulked every window myself last fall. Used the good silicone stuff, too, not that cheap acrylic garbage that cracks after one winter. 

But anyway... what were you asking me? Oh, right, my mood. Yeah, no, I'm not unusually happy or anything. I just can't sit in the recliner for more than five minutes without feeling like I need to jump up and fix something.

symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient mentions losing track of his 10-millimeter sockets and not being able to find his drill battery.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient gets distracted by unrelated thoughts about his grandson, his wife, and caulking windows, temporarily forgetting the doctor's question.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes feeling 'wound up' and unable to sit in his recliner for more than five minutes without needing to jump up.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly states he feels 'like a motor that won't shut off' and has to keep moving.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient gives a long, tangential response, talking excessively about various unrelated topics before returning to the question.
symptom_reasoning.S033: The patient explicitly denies having an elevated mood, stating he is not 'walking on sunshine' or 'unusually happy'.

turns.doctor_question: Before you retired a couple years ago, when you were still working on the construction sites, did you have this same problem with not being able to sit still and always needing to keep moving, or is this something that really started after you stopped working?
turns.patient_response:
Well, you know, it's funny you ask that. See, back on the sites, I was always moving anyway. You don't really have time to sit still when you're managing a crew and trying to keep the subs on schedule. The plumbers, especially—they'll take a three-hour lunch if you don't stay on top of them. I remember this one guy, Sal, great pipefitter, but he'd disappear to get a meatball sub and you wouldn't see him till 2 PM. I had to threaten to tow his truck once just to get him to finish roughing in a master bath. 

But, uh, as far as it being a problem... it really didn't become an issue until after I retired. I stepped away from the handyman work, gosh, about a year and two months ago now. That's when I really noticed it. Because suddenly, I didn't have a schedule, you know? I bought this beautiful leather recliner to celebrate retiring—the kind with the power lumbar support and the cup holders. Thought I was gonna spend my golden years watching old Westerns. Have you seen *Gunsmoke* lately? They run it on that classic channel now. James Arness, what a presence. They don't make actors like that anymore, all tall and stoic. 

But anyway, yeah, I sit in that chair for two minutes and my legs just start bouncing. I gotta get up. So I'd say it really became a real problem a little over a year ago, right after I stopped working.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient states that when he sits down, his 'legs just start bouncing'.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes an internal restlessness, noting he can only sit for two minutes before his legs bounce and he feels he 'gotta get up'.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient confirms the doctor's premise of 'always needing to keep moving', stating it became a real problem after he retired.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient provides a lengthy, rambling response with unnecessary tangential details about a former coworker and a classic TV show.

turns.doctor_question: Going back to when you were a kid in school, or even as a young adult before you started working construction—did you ever have trouble sitting still in class, or did teachers ever say you were fidgety or couldn't focus on one thing?
turns.patient_response:
School? Oh boy, that takes me back. Yeah, even way back in grade school, the teachers always had something to say. They'd tell my parents I was bright, but just... scattered, you know? Always losing my pencils. I swear I went through a pack of those yellow No. 2s a week. The ones with the pink erasers that always smudged the paper if you rubbed too hard. Do they even make those anymore? Now kids just use those mechanical ones, or they do everything on iPads. My grandson, the one I mentioned before, he showed me his homework on this little tablet thing. No paper, no pencil. Just tapping a screen. I don't know how you learn anything if you're not physically writing it down, you know? The muscle memory, that's what cements it in your brain. 

But yeah, my teachers... they were always getting on me. I was the kid who'd just blurt out the answers without raising my hand. I couldn't help it, I just knew the answer and had to get it out. And they were always having to remind me to finish my worksheets before recess. Recess was the only part of the day I actually liked. We used to play kickball on this blacktop that got so hot in the spring you could practically fry an egg on it. I had these PF Flyers—remember those? 'Run faster, jump higher.' I really thought those shoes made me invincible. 

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, school. Yeah, I was definitely fidgety and all over the place back then, too. Just couldn't keep it together to finish a simple math sheet without getting distracted by a bird out the window or something.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient states teachers had to constantly remind him to finish his worksheets.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient recalls frequently losing his pencils in grade school.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient mentions getting easily distracted by things like a bird outside the window.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly confirms he was 'definitely fidgety' as a child.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient admits he would 'blurt out the answers without raising my hand'.

turns.doctor_question: From the time you finished school and started working construction as a young adult, all the way up until you retired a couple years ago—were you still having trouble sitting still and staying focused on tasks during those working years, or did things settle down once you got into your job routine?
turns.patient_response:
Well, like I said, on the sites you don't really sit still much anyway. You're always moving, checking on this, checking on that. But yeah, even then... I guess I was always the guy who couldn't just stand there and watch the concrete cure, you know? I had to be doing something. I remember this one time we were pouring a foundation for a custom build out in the suburbs. Beautiful lot, lots of old oak trees. The kind of trees you just don't see in the new subdivisions because they bulldoze everything flat before they start building. It's a real shame, honestly. They put up these cookie-cutter houses with no character and slap a couple of saplings in the front yard and call it a day. 

Anyway, the concrete truck was late. Driver got lost or something, which happens more than you'd think. So we're all just standing around waiting, and the guys are leaning on their shovels, shooting the breeze, smoking cigarettes. I couldn't do it. I ended up walking the whole perimeter of the lot, picking up trash, organizing the lumber pile, just... doing stuff. I couldn't just stand there and wait. 

But as far as staying focused on tasks... I mean, I got the job done. But I was always bouncing between five different things at once. I'd start framing a wall, then I'd notice a loose wire that the electrician missed, so I'd go fix that, and then I'd see that we were low on nails, so I'd head to the truck... and by the time I got back to the wall, I'd forgotten where my hammer was. Usually left it on the bumper of the truck. I had this great Estwing hammer, solid steel handle, leather grip. Best hammer I ever owned. Had it for fifteen years until some guy swiped it off a job site. You really gotta watch your tools on those bigger commercial jobs, people will walk off with anything that isn't bolted down. 

So yeah, I guess things didn't really settle down, I just... I found a job where being all over the place kind of worked out for me. Until I retired, anyway.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes an inability to sustain attention on a single task, constantly bouncing between multiple tasks like framing a wall and fixing wires.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient mentions frequently losing his hammer by leaving it on the bumper of his truck while working.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient illustrates distractibility by explaining how he would get sidetracked from his main task by noticing unrelated things like a loose wire or low nail supply.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes being constantly in motion on job sites, unable to just stand and wait, and needing to always be doing something.
